meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Never interfere with an enemy while he's in the process of destroying himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Sun Tzu — it isn't in the Art of War. It's a Napoleon-family maxim with no primary source, crystallized in print by Theodore H. White in 1965.

answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — a maxim credited to Napoleon
answer.sourceLine: This line is not in Sun Tzu’s Art of War and is not his. Quote Investigator traces it to a maxim long credited to Napoleon — but finds no primary source in Napoleon’s own words. The exact modern wording about an enemy “destroying himself” was popularized by Theodore H. White’s The Making of the President 1964 (1965), where White himself called it “Napoleon’s maxim.”

source.heading: Where the wording actually comes from
source.excerpt: Never interfere with the enemy when he is in the process of destroying himself.
trail: The line does not appear in Sun Tzu’s Art of War; it is a modern maxim, and the Sun Tzu label is a later internet graft (Quote Investigator).
The oldest kin is an 1836 paraphrase of Napoleon in Archibald Alison’s history — “when the enemy is making a false movement we must take good care not to interrupt him” (QI timeline).
By 1879 a U.S. general presented it simply as a “maxim in war” attached to no famous figure; the near-exact modern wording surfaces in Theodore H. White’s 1965 book (QI).
Even the Napoleon attribution is only “Attributed,” sourced to a 2002 quotation anthology rather than any primary text (Wikiquote: Napoleon).
source.excerptNote: Theodore H. White’s 1965 phrasing — the closest documented match to the popular modern line — which White attributed to “Napoleon’s maxim,” not to Sun Tzu.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is a 20th-century maxim of uncertain, evolved origin rather than a passage from any datable work, so no clean public-domain status can be asserted. Its closest documented print form — Theodore H. White’s The Making of the President 1964 (1965) — is itself in copyright (White estate / Atheneum), and the older Napoleon paraphrases are pre-1931 but do not match this phrasing.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About Napoleon Bonaparte
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte is the figure to whom this battlefield maxim has traditionally been pinned since the 19th century, though no primary source in his own words has ever been found. The idea — let a blundering opponent blunder — suits his reputation, which is exactly why the line accreted to him, and later to Sun Tzu. The specific modern phrasing about an enemy “destroying himself” is a 20th-century crystallization popularized by journalist Theodore H. White.

misattribution.heading: How Sun Tzu got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is a modern battlefield maxim with no anchor in any classical text. It has drifted between famous strategists — and the internet increasingly hangs it on Sun Tzu.

items.why: The phrase appears nowhere in the Art of War; Quote Investigator’s investigation of the maxim does not mention Sun Tzu at all. It is grafted onto his name because he is a magnet for strategy-flavored quotes.
Widely credited to Napoleon since the 1800s, but only as a paraphrase — no primary text in his own words exists, and Wikiquote files it as merely Attributed.

misattribution.truthLine: The safest statement: it is a folk maxim of the Napoleonic-quote tradition whose exact modern wording was popularized by Theodore H. White in 1965 — and it is not Sun Tzu’s (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The maxim compresses a real strategic principle: an opponent already blundering into ruin should be left to it, not jolted awake by interference. That timeless-sounding logic is exactly what makes it so easy to hang on an ancient sage.

Quote Investigator shows the phrasing evolving for over a century — from an 1836 paraphrase of Napoleon, to an unattributed “maxim in war” by 1879, to Theodore H. White’s near-exact 1965 wording — long after Sun Tzu, and never actually in his hand.
context.pull: Not in the Art of War, not Napoleon’s documented words — a maxim that grew into its famous names.
